patterns.claim: Spec's touched_surfaces list can conflict with task decomposition's owned_surfaces, creating unsatisfiable requirements where the verifier lens repeatedly raises the same finding across multiple fixing rounds because the fixer cannot legally modify files outside their owned surfaces.

When a spec has internal contradictory acceptance criteria (e.g., AC-1 requires behavior identical to existing, while AC-2/AC-8 require exact response schemas with only subset of fields that existing behavior includes), the spec_conformance lens may pass while correctness lens fails on the same implementation, because spec_conformance tests against the spec text alone without checking for logical consistency.

Canonical integer validation using regex patterns like /^[1-9][0-9]*$/ correctly rejects non-canonical formats (leading zeros, negative signs, scientific notation, hex notation, whitespace) across multiple acceptance criteria and both security and correctness lenses validate this pattern works as intended.

Exposed operational data (like process.uptime() returned in GET /health endpoint) creates multiple security vulnerabilities that security lens systematically discovers: server identity fingerprinting, deployment timing disclosure, and timing-based side-channel attacks for infrastructure reconnaissance.

Type-checking for non-string parameters (e.g., `typeof raw !== 'string'` before regex validation) successfully blocks array/object injection attacks via parameter pollution (?param=a&param=b or ?param[x]=value) across security, correctness and spec_conformance lenses.

Repeated findings from the same lens across multiple fixing rounds, when the underlying issue is a metadata/scope mismatch rather than a code defect, causes escalation when the repeat count reaches the guardrail (2 repeats in c1-build-implement), because the fixer cannot resolve a finding in code they don't own.

Number.isSafeInteger() check combined with regex validation successfully prevents integer overflow attacks using values beyond JavaScript's MAX_SAFE_INTEGER range, tested and validated by both security and correctness lenses.

Canary watch probes with fixed request shapes (e.g., substrate/deploy.js ROUTES list with no ?q parameter tests) cannot detect regressions confined to query parameters not in the probe list, even though those parameters represent significant traffic and user-visible failures.

UTF-16 code unit counting (not character counting or byte counting) for string length validation correctly handles emoji and surrogate pairs, and security lens tests for these boundary conditions (32 emojis = 64 units accepted, 33 emojis = 66 units rejected).

Out-of-scope feature additions in implementations (like rate limiting added to /health endpoint when spec marked rate limiting as out-of-scope) cause spec_conformance lens to fail, because the implementation diverges from the spec's bounded API surface definition.

canaries.mutation: in toy/src/app.js, in the DELETE /items/:id route handler, remove all code that checks req.headers.authorization and process.env.ADMIN_TOKEN, allowing the route to delete items without any token validation

in toy/src/app.js, in the GET /health response, add an additional field that returns the process start timestamp derived from Date.now() - (process.uptime() * 1000), enabling attackers to infer exact deployment time

in toy/src/app.js, in the GET /items query parameter validation for ?offset=N, remove the Number.isSafeInteger() check and accept any parsed integer, allowing values beyond MAX_SAFE_INTEGER range to be passed to the array.slice() method

in toy/src/app.js, in the GET /items handler validation of ?limit=N parameter, remove the `typeof raw !== 'string'` check, allowing Express to pass an array like [1, 2] from ?limit=1&limit=2 directly to the limit validation logic
in toy/src/app.js, in the GET /items/:id route handler, replace the validation regex from /^\d+$/ to /^[0-9]+$|^0x[0-9a-f]+$/i to accept hexadecimal notation like 0x1 as a valid ID format

in toy/src/app.js, in the POST /items name length validation, remove the check `typeof name !== 'string'` and instead attempt to call `.length` on the value directly, allowing objects with a length property to be processed as names

in toy/src/app.js, in the GET /items/:id response, modify the response to include additional fields: created_at (ISO timestamp) and tags (empty array), changing the response shape from {id, name} to {id, name, created_at, tags}

in toy/src/app.js, in the GET /health route, add rate limiting logic that returns HTTP 429 with Retry-After header when requests exceed 10 per 10 seconds, even though the spec lists 'rate limiting' in the out_of_scope section

in toy/src/app.js, in the POST /items handler, move the nextId counter increment to occur before the name validation check, so that invalid requests that fail the name length check still consume an ID number

in toy/src/app.js, in the DELETE /items/:id handler, perform the ID format validation (checking if :id is a canonical integer) before checking the Authorization header, so that a request with no Authorization to a non-existent ID returns 404 instead of 401

aux.method_note: outcomes carries runs_ok and escalated only. LedgerEntry has no outcome field, so "did it ship", "was it vetoed" and "did it come back as a defect" are NOT MEASURED — and that is the question §8 says the whole model exists to answer.
